# Meet-in-the-Middle Subset-Sum – Student B notes

**How the problem is divided.** The n numbers are split into two halves of n/2 numbers. Any subset is the union of a subset of the first half and a subset of the second half, so a subset with sum T exists exactly when some sum `a` from the first half and some sum `b` from the second half satisfy a + b = T.

**Subset results.** Each half has 2^(n/2) subsets; their sums are generated by repeated doubling of a list (`sums += [s + x for s in sums]`).

**Combining.** Sort both lists, then use two pointers – one moving up the first list, one moving down the second – to look for a + b = T in at most 2·2^(n/2) steps (sorting adds O(2^(n/2)·n) time).

**Search-space size.** 2 × 2^(n/2) = 2^(n/2 + 1) sums instead of 2^n subsets. For n = 40: 2,097,152 sums instead of 1,099,511,627,776 subsets.

**Memory.** Θ(2^(n/2)) stored sums (n = 32: 131,072 sums, ~6 MB measured in Python; n = 60 would need about 2^31 sums ≈ 17 GB even at 8 bytes each). Naive Gray-code enumeration needs only O(n) memory.

**Trade-off.** Time falls from 2^n to about 2^(n/2) but memory grows from O(n) to O(2^(n/2)). With limited memory the usable n is bounded by memory, not time.

**Measured speed-up (unreachable target, full search):** 88× at n = 16, 361× at n = 20, 1,450× at n = 24; naive enumeration was not run beyond n = 24, while MITM handled n = 40 in about a second.
